title: Ventilating Status Asthmaticus
keywords: minimise minute ventilation not airway pressure
watch expiratory flow return to zero
sedation paralysis to prevent fighting hypoventilation
sources: Critical Vector — Vent Pocket Guide: Status Asthmaticus
Standard critical-care references on near-fatal asthma; the strategy rests on physiologic reasoning and case series, not RCT

changelog.change: Initial entry — the controlled-hypoventilation strategy, initial settings, the monitoring triad, and the sedation/paralysis point.

summary: This is NOT ARDS ventilation. The lung is not stiff — it is obstructed. The goal is to MINIMISE minute ventilation so an obstructed lung has time to fully exhale, accepting a high PaCO2 and a low pH. High peak pressures from airway resistance are tolerable; the plateau pressure is what matters.

body.text: The enemy is dynamic hyperinflation (breath stacking / auto-PEEP), which causes hypotension and barotrauma. If the patient becomes hypotensive on the ventilator: DISCONNECT the circuit and let them exhale (chest deflates over 20–60 s), give fluid, then resume with an even lower rate. Rule out tension pneumothorax.

items: Tidal volume 5–8 mL/kg predicted body weight (deliberately on the low side).
Respiratory rate 10–14/min — deliberately low, to lengthen expiratory time.
High inspiratory flow 60–100 L/min (shortens inspiratory time, maximises expiratory time). A square/constant flow pattern.
PEEP low (0–5). Extrinsic PEEP does not help the deeply obstructed asthmatic and can worsen hyperinflation.
Tolerate pH > 7.20; extreme cases have been managed to pH < 7.0 without apparent harm. Sodium bicarbonate is not routinely needed and can worsen intracellular acidosis.

rows: Expiratory flow NOT returning to zero before the next breath = breath stacking
The best bedside surrogate for alveolar pressure — target < 30 cmH2O — even while PIP runs high from resistance
Direct markers of dynamic hyperinflation; trend them as you adjust the rate

body.text: Deep sedation, and usually a short course of neuromuscular blockade, are needed to stop the patient from fighting a strategy that deliberately hypoventilates them. Continue aggressive bronchodilators (continuous nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium), IV/IM magnesium, systemic steroids, and consider IV/IM adrenaline or an inhalational anaesthetic / ECMO in the refractory patient.
